reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Defined as blood in the anterior chamber, usually seen as a layered red fluid level in the inferior chamber when the patient is upright
Most commonly follows blunt ocular trauma, but spontaneous hyphema should prompt consideration of neovascularisation, tumour, or a bleeding tendency
Grading is by the height of the layered blood; a total chamber filled with dark clotted blood is termed an eight-ball hyphema
Raised intraocular pressure is a major early concern, particularly in sickle cell disease where even modest pressures endanger the optic nerve
Rebleeding, typically within the first several days, tends to be more severe than the original bleed and worsens prognosis
Management principles include rest with head elevation, limiting activity, shielding the eye, and close monitoring of pressure; avoiding antiplatelet and anticoagulant agents where possible
Corneal blood staining and glaucoma are the main sight-threatening complications requiring surgical washout if uncontrolled
All patients of African, Mediterranean, or Middle Eastern descent should be screened for sickle cell status
reference.pathophysiology: Hyphema results from disruption of iris or ciliary body vessels, most often by blunt trauma that causes rapid globe compression and a sudden shift of intraocular structures, tearing vessels at the iris root or angle. Red cells settle inferiorly under gravity. Clot formation and subsequent fibrinolysis create a window of rebleeding risk. Blood and inflammatory debris obstruct the trabecular meshwork, raising intraocular pressure; in sickle cell disease, red cells sickle in the low-oxygen, acidotic aqueous, further impairing outflow and increasing susceptibility to optic nerve damage. Prolonged high pressure with an intact endothelial insult leads to corneal blood staining.
additionalDifferentials: Neovascular disease (diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, ocular ischaemia)
Intraocular tumour (e.g. retinoblastoma in children, melanoma)
Herpetic or other uveitis with bleeding
Juvenile xanthogranuloma of the iris in children
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination to grade the hyphema and detect associated trauma
Intraocular pressure measurement and serial monitoring
Gonioscopy (deferred until rebleeding risk passes) to assess angle recession
Dilated fundus examination or B-scan ultrasound if the view is obscured, to exclude posterior segment injury
Sickle cell screening in at-risk patients
Coagulation studies when a bleeding tendency is suspected
redFlags: Uncontrolled raised intraocular pressure threatening the optic nerve, especially in sickle cell disease
Rebleeding with a larger, darker hyphema
Early corneal blood staining indicating endothelial compromise
Signs of globe rupture or associated posterior segment injury
Spontaneous hyphema in a child raising concern for retinoblastoma
reference.prognosis: Small hyphemas usually clear without sequelae, but larger bleeds, rebleeding, sickle cell disease, and sustained pressure elevation carry a higher risk of glaucoma, corneal staining, and permanent visual loss.
pitfalls: Failing to screen for sickle cell disease, in which tolerable pressures for others become sight-threatening
Missing associated injuries such as angle recession, lens dislocation, or globe rupture
Underestimating rebleeding risk and permitting excessive activity
Overlooking a spontaneous hyphema as a marker of neovascular disease or tumour
